\smallskip
\begin{minipage}{\linewidth}\footnotesize\raggedright
Medians over the instances (the iterations, from the zero field / to the prediction's accuracy, and CG's displacement error: over the load cases). 2D: the first 32 validation instances of the two-dimensional comparison, with its label-free transformer of seed 0; 3D: the first 32 validation and the first 8 fine-mesh instances of the three-dimensional comparison, with its label-free transformer of seed 0. Times are wall times per instance, for all its load cases together; assembly is excluded from both sides (the surrogate needs no stiffness matrix).\par
The surrogate ran on one NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5090 with TF32; both its rows include preparing the inputs and copying the prediction back, the first call after an untimed warm-up on 4 validation instances, the repeated one as the median of 2 further passes. The solvers ran on the CPU of the same machine (Xeon Gold 6459C, 16 CPUs, the thread environment set to 16): SuperLU, which produced the labels, and unpreconditioned conjugate gradients (CG) to a relative residual of $10^{-10}$, from the zero field or from the prediction. CG to the prediction's accuracy starts from the zero field and stops, on each load case, at the first iterate whose relative energy error is at most the prediction's: a stop that reads the reference solution, so a lower bound.\par
On the fine mesh, three of the 32 load cases had a relative energy gap above 1 (4.76, 4.77 and 22.0) and three of the eight instances a mean above 1; CG matches such a load case with no iteration.\par
Threads, on a second host (Xeon Platinum 8470Q, 25 threads), first 8 validation and 2 fine-mesh 3D instances: with one thread, the direct solve took the same time (within 1.1\%) and CG 16\%--29\% less; a repeat with 25 threads agreed within 2.1\%. In 2D (8 instances, no repeat), one thread was 7.2\% faster for the direct solve and 4.3\% for CG.
\end{minipage}
\end{table}
